citation: Effendy I, Gelber A, Lehmann P, Huledal G, Lillieborg S. Plasma concentrations and analgesic efficacy of lidocaine and prilocaine in leg ulcer-related pain during daily application of lidocaine-prilocaine cream (EMLA) for 10 days. Br J Dermatol 2015;173(1):259-261 (research letter).
text_quality: ok: all 3 PDF pages, tables, figure legend and references complete. Extraction drops decimal points ('P < 0001' is P < 0.001) and superscript minus signs; PDF pages 2 and 3 were rendered to check Fig. 1 and the P values. PubMed has no abstract for this letter.
design: Open, uncontrolled, multicentre clinical study published as a research letter. Primary aim pharmacokinetic (sample size set to estimate the 90th percentile of the summed peak plasma concentration of lidocaine and prilocaine with a one-sided upper confidence bound); secondary aim the course of chronic ulcer pain. No placebo, comparator or control arm. The letter states no limitations; not stated by the authors but evident from the design: the pain course is confounded by concurrent sharp debridement, dressings, compression and regular analgesics (opioids in 8 of 14 analgesic users). Internal inconsistency: methods give pre-dose sampling on days 2, 4, 6 and 8, results report pre-dose samples on days 3, 5, 7 and 9; the text gives P < 0.001 for the pain fall, the Table 1 footnote P < 0.01.
population: 25 adult inpatients with leg ulcers present at least 6 weeks: 23 needing sharp debridement and 2 not needing it but with chronic ulcer pain. Aetiology venous 17, arteriovenous 5, vasculitic 3; median age 71; 6 men, 19 women. 15 of 25 had moderate or severe chronic ulcer pain at enrolment (verbal rating scale). No patient is described as having neuropathic pain: the words neuropathic, neuropathy and neuralgia do not occur in the letter, and no diabetic or neuropathic ulcer is listed.
n: 25 (debridement n = 23; non-debridement n = 2). Pain-course analysis: patients with moderate or severe pain at enrolment (15 reported such pain; one non-debridement patient with slight pain was excluded). Ulcer-area analysis excluded 3 patients in whom only part of the ulcer was treated.
setting: Inpatients at five departments of dermatology in Germany (Bielefeld, Wuppertal, Homburg-Saar, Bonn, Lemgo); sponsor AstraZeneca.
intervention: Lidocaine-prilocaine eutectic cream (EMLA) applied once a day for ten days to the ulcer in a thick layer under cling film, wiped off after one hour, followed by sharp curette debridement on days 1-5 and up to day 10 when indicated; for large ulcers only a capped part of the ulcer was treated and the rest protected with a paste dressing (amount of cream and size of the capped area: [dose figure omitted]). Hydrocolloid or silicone dressings between treatments; compression bandages on venous ulcers. Exposure duration, asked by claim D066: about one hour of contact per application, daily for ten days, i.e. about ten hours of cumulative contact; the letter gives no cumulative figure itself.
comparator: None (uncontrolled); within-patient comparison of day 10 with day 1.
route: Topical, on ulcerated (broken) skin of the leg, under occlusion with cling film.
duration: Ten days of daily application; blood sampling to four hours after the first (day 1) and last (day 10) application, plus pre-dose samples on alternate days; ulcer area on days 1 and 10.
outcomes: Plasma lidocaine and prilocaine (LC-MS/MS) serially after the first (day 1) and last (day 10) application and before application on alternate days; peak concentration (Cmax) day 1 vs day 10 with two-sided 95% CIs; 90th percentile of the summed Cmax with a one-sided upper confidence limit; regression of Cmax on age, ulcer area, ulcer type and day; current ulcer pain rated daily before each application on a 100-mm VAS ruler (the first of several unspecified 'standard questions'); verbal rating scale of chronic ulcer pain at enrolment; ulcer area on days 1 and 10; observed symptoms of systemic local-anaesthetic toxicity. Not measured or not reported: methaemoglobin (no measurement; the letter mentions methaemoglobinaemia only as a general property of parenteral prilocaine), pain during debridement, quantitative sensory testing, any neuropathic-pain measure.

key_results.quote: We report a study designed to determine the plasma concentrations of lidocaine and prilocaine during repeated daily application, for 10 days, of [dose figure omitted] EMLA to leg ulcers, and to evaluate the analgesic effect on chronic ulcer pain.
This open study, conducted at five departments of dermatology in Germany, was approved by the relevant local ethics committees.
Patients were asked standard questions each day before the application of EMLA. The first question was ‘Please rate the current intensity of the pain from your ulcer using the pain ruler’.

After 1 h, any remaining cream was wiped away and sharp debridement by a disposable curette (Stiefel, Research Triangle Park, NC, U.S.A.) performed for the first 5 days and, when indicated for achieving a clean ulcer, for up to 10 days.

Twenty-five patients participated, of whom 15 (60%) reported on enrolment chronic ulcer pain of moderate or severe intensity (Table 1). Eight of the 14 patients who regularly used analgesics for ulcer pain were prescribed opioids.
No symptoms of systemic local anaesthetic toxicity were observed.

Cmax values observed at similar time points were similar on days 1 and 10 for lidocaine, prilocaine, and the sum of lidocaine and prilocaine concentrations (Fig. 1), with the two-sided 95% CI for each difference between day 1 and day 10 values including zero
The size of the ulcer area had a significant effect (P < 001) on the peak values.
Cmax values did not depend on patient age (P > 070) or ulcer type (P > 050).

Mean predose samples taken before EMLA application on days 3, 5, 7 and 9 were [dose figure omitted] for lidocaine and prilocaine, respectively, indicating minimal residual concentrations 24 h after the previous treatment.
In patients with moderate or severe chronic ulcer pain, prior to enrolment the median pretreatment VAS pain score was 75, which decreased gradually to 21 by day 10 (P < 0001).
The sum of plasma concentrations of lidocaine and prilocaine shows no apparent accumulation over 10 days

author_limitations.quote: suggesting that the use of EMLA in patients with painful leg ulcers deserves further study

funding_conflicts: Funded by AstraZeneca (maker of EMLA). S. Lillieborg is an AstraZeneca employee; G. Huledal was an AstraZeneca employee during the study. The power calculation is credited to biostatistician Jan Henriksson. The only author caveat is the call for further study of the cream in painful leg ulcers, made about a case report (Purcell 2012); no limitations section.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Lok C, Paul C, Amblard P, et al. EMLA cream as a topical anesthetic for the repeated mechanical debridement of venous leg ulcers: a double-blind, placebo-controlled study. J Am Acad Dermatol 1999;40:208-13.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 69 patients, cream before repeated debridements; plasma lidocaine, prilocaine and their main metabolites measured across the repeated sessions, without apparent accumulation. Bears on C070 (repeated prilocaine across sessions) and D072 (accumulation measured between repeated sessions, topical route).

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Hansson C, Holm J, Lillieborg S, Syren A. Repeated treatment with lidocaine/prilocaine cream (EMLA) as a topical anaesthetic for the cleansing of venous leg ulcers. A controlled study. Acta Derm Venereol 1993;73:231-3.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Randomised controlled study of a series of repeated EMLA treatments vs control before ulcer cleansing; local reactions scored at every treatment, granulation tissue, ulcer area and bacterial flora at first and last; analgesic effect unchanged with successive treatments. Bears on C070 (local tissue change and maintained effect across repeated sessions, topical).

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Enander Malmros I, Nilsen T, Lillieborg S. Plasma concentrations and analgesic effect of EMLA (lidocaine/prilocaine) cream for the cleansing of leg ulcers. Acta Derm Venereol 1990;70:227-30.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Plasma lidocaine and prilocaine after a single one-hour application to leg ulcers (8 patients), plus a double-blind four-period crossover of two cream strengths across four consecutive debridements (10 patients); Effendy's source for the bioavailability estimate. Plasma levels after topical anaesthetics on broken skin; repeated sessions.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Holm J, Andren B, Grafford K. Pain control in the surgical debridement of leg ulcers by the use of a topical lidocaine-prilocaine cream, EMLA. Acta Derm Venereol 1990;70:132-6.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Open study and double-blind placebo comparison, 80 patients with venous or arterial ulcers; procedural pain on a 100-mm VAS and plasma lidocaine and prilocaine measured. Topical anaesthetic analgesia and plasma levels on ulcers.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Agrifoglio G, Domanin M, Baggio E, et al. EMLA anaesthetic cream for sharp debridement of venous leg ulcers. A double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Phlebology 2000;15:81-3.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Placebo-controlled trial of the cream for debridement pain; not indexed in PubMed (author search returns 0).

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Rosenthal D, Murphy F, Gottschalk R, et al. Using a topical anaesthetic cream to reduce pain during sharp debridement of chronic leg ulcers. J Wound Care 2001;10:503-5.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, 101 patients with arterial, venous or arteriovenous ulcers; debridement pain on VAS; local reactions in similar proportions with placebo.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Briggs M, Nelson EA, Martyn-St James M. Topical agents or dressings for pain in venous leg ulcers. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;11:CD001177.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Cochrane review: six trials (343 participants) of the cream for debridement pain; calls for research on long-term use. Topical anaesthetics for wound pain.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Purcell A, Marshall A, King J, Buckley T. J Wound Care 2012;21:309-10 (case report: EMLA cream as a primary dressing on a painful lower leg ulcer).
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Single case of the cream used as a continuing primary dressing on a painful leg ulcer, pain falling over three weeks. Precursor of the same group's pilot randomised trial of daily use for four weeks (Purcell 2017, PMID 28727591; not cited by Effendy). Repeated/daily topical use for chronic pain; bears on D066 context and C070.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Aps C, Reynolds F. The effect of concentration on vasoactivity of bupivacaine and lignocaine. Br J Anaesth 1976;48:1171-4.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Double-blind intradermal volunteer study (31 volunteers), bupivacaine and lidocaine each at three concentrations: vasoconstriction more frequent at low and vasodilatation at high concentrations; duration of action unaffected by concentration except at the highest bupivacaine strength. One of the Reynolds-group intradermal studies; bears on skin vasoactivity and duration in the lidocaine, bupivacaine and wheal-comparison pages. Effendy cites it for the biphasic vascular effect behind transient pallor or erythema of the ulcer.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.citation: Covino BG, Wildsmith JAW. Clinical pharmacology of local anesthetic agents. In: Cousins MJ, Bridenbaugh PO, eds. Neural Blockade in Clinical Anesthesia and Management of Pain, 3rd edn. Lippincott-Raven, 1998:97-128.
studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Textbook chapter Effendy cites for the plasma level associated with central nervous system toxicity (figure not copied). Plasma levels and systemic toxicity.

studies_it_cites_that_matter.why: Prevalence and severity of pain in venous leg ulcers (background for chronic wound pain; no claim found on this topic).
